title: Leading Lady vs. Glamorise at 46A: Why band, cup, and bra shape all need checking
summary: A recent search for a 46A exposed a real gap between a shopper's size and many brands' product grids. Leading Lady currently lists multiple 46A styles, while a comparable Glamorise range starts at B—yet availability is only the first fit question.
author: Curvy& Editorial

sections.heading: The hard-to-find size is a range problem, not a body problem
paragraphs: A recent r/PlusSizeFashion thread attracted a substantial response around a shopper's frustration finding a 46A or 48A in a conventional bra rather than only sports-bra-style options. The post named several familiar plus-size retailers that did not solve the search. Replies offered sister sizes, extenders, new measurement methods, and less structured cups, but they did not establish one size or style that would work for the original poster.

That distinction matters. Large band and smaller cup combinations are legitimate size needs, but not every brand builds every cup on every band. A missing 46A is an inventory-grid decision; it does not prove the measurement is wrong. At the same time, repeated gaping, riding, or discomfort is a reason to recheck both size and shape before spending on the few available products.

sections.heading: Remeasure before translating the label
paragraphs: A Bra That Fits uses six measurements: loose, snug, and tight underbust plus standing, leaning, and lying bust. Its calculator and beginner guide describe the result as a starting point rather than a guarantee. That is especially useful when a person has been assigned one size from a single overbust-and-underbust method but experiences a riding band, empty molded cup, spillage, or wires that do not follow the breast root.

The six-measurement approach can produce a cup letter that looks surprising because cup letters are relative to band size, not fixed descriptions of breast volume. The ABTF guide also notes that shape is half the fit problem: breast tissue can be distributed shallowly across a wider or taller root or project more deeply from a narrower root. Two people with the same label may therefore need very different cup constructions.

Measurement is not a verdict about how breasts should look. Use the calculator result, the current bra's fit symptoms, and comfort together. If a calculated size differs substantially from what you own, test nearby sizes in one consistent style instead of replacing an entire drawer at once.

sections.heading: Leading Lady and Glamorise publish different product grids
paragraphs: Leading Lady currently maintains dedicated 46A collections for underwire, wireless, front-closure, and T-shirt bras. Its 46A T-shirt-bra page shows multiple Brigitte variants, the Luna front-closure racerback, and other shapes. The brand's fit tool instructs shoppers to measure the torso directly under the breasts for the band and the fullest bust area for the cup, then use the product-specific size chart where alpha sizing appears.

Glamorise's current Front-Closure WonderWire product provides a useful contrast. Its published grid includes band 46 in B through H, but not A. That does not mean Glamorise has no possible garment for every small-bust shopper or that its B will fit like Leading Lady's A. It means this specific conventional band-and-cup product cannot be ordered in 46A, so a shopper must either test a justified neighboring size or choose a brand and style that actually makes the measured starting point.

The comparison also shows why a brand-level maximum is incomplete. A company may sell wide band ranges overall while an individual style begins at B, C, or a grouped stretch-cup size. Always confirm the exact color and product variant because availability can change within a style.
bullets: Leading Lady: current dedicated listings show multiple 46A underwire, wireless, front-close, and T-shirt options.
Glamorise Front-Closure WonderWire: current published range includes 46B–46H, not 46A.
Editorial conclusion: compare the exact style grid before comparing price, padding, or appearance.

sections.heading: A cup can gap because of shape, not only excess volume
paragraphs: Leading Lady's Brigitte examples are lightly padded, contoured, full-coverage T-shirt bras. A molded cup holds its own shape, which creates a smooth outline when the body's breast root, projection, and fullness match the mold. When they do not match, the edge can stand away even if part of the cup is too shallow or the wire is too wide. Automatically moving to a smaller cup may trade visible space for new pressure elsewhere.

An unlined or stretch-cup bra conforms more readily, but it creates a different silhouette and may show seams under thin clothing. Glamorise's WonderWire example uses seamed cups and cushioned underwire rather than a seamless molded T-shirt construction. Because the Glamorise page begins at B on a 46 band, it is a construction comparison—not evidence that 46B preserves the same cup volume as 46A.

When trying any bra, assess the band independently by fastening it upside down and backward so the cups are out of the way. Then put it on normally, position all tissue into the cups, and check whether the band stays level, the cup contains without cutting or wrinkling, the wire follows rather than sits on breast tissue, and the center gore behaves comfortably. Comfort remains the deciding criterion.

sections.heading: Sister sizing is a controlled test, not a universal workaround
paragraphs: Sister sizing changes the band and cup letter together to preserve approximately the same cup volume: moving down one band from 46A leads to 44B. It can be useful when the original band feels loose or a particular style runs long. It is not equivalent sizing in every dimension. The 44 band is shorter, the wires and strap placement may change, and a person whose underbust truly needs 46 may find it uncomfortable.

A band extender changes the starting circumference of a bra but does not enlarge the cup or reposition its wires. It can make a firm new 44B more wearable during a controlled trial, but it cannot solve a cup that is the wrong shape or volume. Conversely, moving to 46B keeps the same band and increases cup volume; it is not the sister size of 46A.

Test only one variable at a time. If the 46A band rides up while the cups behave well, compare with 44B in the same model. If the band is stable but the molded cup gaps, try another cup construction before assuming the label must shrink. If there is spillage or the wire sits on tissue, more cup room or a different shape may be required even when the breasts look small relative to the torso.

sections.heading: Build a low-risk first order
paragraphs: Begin with the measured starting size in a style whose size grid actually includes it. Leading Lady's current 46A range makes that possible across several closure and wire choices. Choose one construction based on the fit problem you are trying to solve: seamless contour for a smooth T-shirt line, an unlined or more flexible cup for easier shape accommodation, front closure for dressing access, or wireless construction when wire comfort is the main concern.

Order adjacent sizes only when each one tests a specific hypothesis. A 44B asks whether a shorter band with similar cup volume is better; a 46B asks whether the same band needs more cup volume. A different 46A style asks whether the label is reasonable but the original cup shape was not. Record the answer separately for band, cup, wire, straps, gore, and overall comfort.

Check return eligibility on the exact item before purchase, particularly when a color is discounted or final sale. Keep tags attached during a brief indoor fit test and avoid judging solely from cleavage or the label. The best result is not proof that one brand is universally true to size; it is a repeatable understanding of which measurements and constructions work for your body.
bullets: Take all six ABTF measurements and treat the result as a starting point.
Confirm that the exact brand, style, and color are made in the target size.
Choose molded, seamed, stretch-cup, wired, or wireless construction deliberately.
Use 44B versus 46A only to test a shorter band at similar cup volume.
Document fit by component and return unsuitable bras within the seller's current terms.

researchNote: This article responds to an August 2026 public discussion about finding 46A and 48A bras. It verifies current size availability and construction on official Leading Lady and Glamorise pages and uses the A Bra That Fits calculator and beginner guide for measurement and fit concepts. Community advice is not treated as a diagnosis or consensus; bra comfort and fit vary by measurements, tissue distribution, product construction, and personal preference.
